What Pricing Signals

A reading on why the number on the price page is never just a number, and what happens to a company when it forgets that.

1. A Tuesday in Bangalore, and a number that would not sit still

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meera Iyer, vice-president of product at a Bangalore analytics company called Nirveda Analytics, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for a week. Nirveda sold a product that watched a company's transactional data and flagged anomalies before they became write-offs — duplicate vendor payments, quietly escalating discount approvals, invoices that did not match purchase orders. The product worked. Forty-one mid-market customers used it, mostly finance-operations teams at manufacturing and logistics firms with revenues between ₹200 crore and ₹1,500 crore. The question in front of Meera was not whether the product worked. It was what to charge for it, and she had three numbers on the screen, each defensible, each producing a different company.

The first number, ₹18,000 a month per business unit, was what the sales team wanted: low enough that a finance controller could approve it without a procurement committee, priced to spread fast through mid-market accounts the way a expense-management tool might. The second, ₹65,000 a month with a named customer-success manager included, was what the two enterprise pilots in the pipeline — a steel distributor in Pune and a logistics group in Chennai — were half-expecting, because that was roughly what they paid for their fraud-analytics incumbent. The third was not a number at all but a formula: 0.4 basis points of the transaction volume the product screened, which made the bill scale with the customer's exposure and, not incidentally, with Nirveda's own inference cost, since every screened transaction meant a call to the anomaly-detection model. The board meeting was six weeks away. Meera's problem was that she kept treating this as an arithmetic exercise — what does it cost us, what will the market bear — when a colleague from Nirveda's original seed investor, a operating partner named Arvind Seshadri who had built pricing for two prior SaaS companies, told her over coffee that she was solving the wrong problem first. "Before you ask what to charge," he said, "ask what each of those three numbers tells a CFO about who you think you are." That sentence is the subject of this reading.

2. The idea, defined precisely

A price signal is the information a price carries about a product's quality, its intended buyer, and the seller's confidence in it — information the buyer receives before, and sometimes instead of, any direct evidence about the product itself. The idea rests on a simple observation from economics: when a buyer cannot fully verify quality in advance (this condition is called information asymmetry), they use observable proxies to infer what they cannot check directly, and price is one of the most visible proxies available. The formal groundwork was laid by the economist Michael Spence in 1973, in work on labour markets that later won a Nobel Prize, where he showed that a costly, hard-to-fake action — there, a university degree — could credibly signal quality that could not otherwise be observed before hiring. Marketing scholars, notably Kent Monroe in a string of papers through the 1970s and Akshay Rao more recently, applied the same logic to price: a buyer facing two unfamiliar brands of the same product will, absent other information, often infer that the more expensive one is better made, because charging more only makes sense for a seller who can back it up.

What this idea was invented to solve is the gap between what a seller knows about their own product and what a buyer can verify before purchase. A buyer meeting Nirveda Analytics for the first time cannot run the anomaly-detection model against five years of their own transaction history before signing a contract; they infer quality from cues, and price is one of the loudest cues in the room, alongside brand, packaging, and who else buys it. This is different from, and often confused with, the idea that price simply reflects cost or demand. Cost tells the seller what they must charge to survive; demand curves tell an economist how volume responds to price; a price signal is about the inference the price produces in the buyer's mind regardless of what generated the number. The sentence Meera could say in the board meeting without sounding glib is this: our price is the clearest claim we make about who we think we are and who we built this for — read before a single feature is.

This concept builds directly on two ideas the reader has likely already met. The first is packaging — the practice of arranging good, better, and best tiers so that the tiers themselves tell a customer which one is meant for them. Packaging says who you're for through the shape of the offer; price signalling says the same thing through the number attached to it, and the two must agree or the signal breaks. The second is positioning — the broader claim a company makes about which customers it serves and what alternative it replaces. Positioning is a strategic statement, usually made in words, in a pitch deck or a homepage headline. A price signal is that same statement made measurable: it is positioning that a customer can look up, compare, and act on in thirty seconds, without reading a word of the marketing copy.

3. The mechanics, walked through

Price signalling has a mechanism, and skipping steps in it is exactly what produces the confusion Meera was sitting in. The first step is that a buyer forms a reference price — an expectation of what a product like this should cost, built from category norms, from what they already pay for adjacent tools, and from any anchor the seller has planted, such as a "starting at" figure on a website. For the Pune steel distributor evaluating Nirveda, the reference price was set by their existing fraud-analytics vendor, an established audit-software firm charging roughly ₹60,000 a month; any Nirveda number would be read against that anchor, not in isolation.

The second step is that the buyer compares the actual price to that reference and asks, consciously or not, what kind of product costs this much. A price meaningfully below the reference triggers one of two inferences: either the seller has found a genuine efficiency the buyer should welcome, or the product is missing something the reference product has. Which inference wins depends on a third step, congruence — whether every other signal the buyer receives (the sales process, the website design, the size of the support team, the confidence of the salesperson) is consistent with the price. A ₹18,000 price delivered by a founder personally walking a CFO through a slow, hand-holding sales cycle sends two contradictory signals at once, and buyers resolve contradictions by trusting the cheaper-looking cue, usually the price. This is the step practitioners most often skip: they set the number and assume the rest of the go-to-market motion will simply follow it, when in fact every touchpoint is broadcasting a price signal of its own, and they must all agree.

The fourth step, easy to miss, is that the signal is read not just by the buyer in front of the seller but by everyone the buyer talks to next — a peer at another company, a procurement officer benchmarking vendors, an analyst covering the category. A price is public in a way a feature roadmap is not; it becomes part of how the whole market talks about the company. The fifth and final step is durability: once a price has been quoted, discounted, or renegotiated in front of a customer, that customer's reference price shifts permanently downward, and the signal for every future interaction with them is now anchored to the discount, not the list price. This is why the mechanics of price signalling are inseparable from discipline in discounting — a point the worked example below makes concrete.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Return to Nirveda's three numbers, and put real unit economics under each one, because a price signal that the company cannot actually afford to honour is a promise it will break within a year. Nirveda's inference cost — the compute spent calling its anomaly-detection model against a customer's transactions — averaged ₹4,200 per business unit per month at the volumes its mid-market customers ran, based on actual cloud billing Meera pulled for August 2026. Support cost, allocated per account, ran another ₹3,100 a month for the self-serve tier and roughly ₹11,000 a month for accounts with a named customer-success manager, because those accounts consumed real human hours in onboarding and quarterly reviews.

The self-serve number covered costs comfortably but signalled, correctly, that Nirveda was a tool rather than a system of record — fine for the mid-market base, wrong for the two enterprise pilots who expected a partner, not a subscription. The enterprise number was the only one whose signal and unit economics agreed with each other for the accounts it was aimed at.

Now run the second pass, changing one input: suppose a competitor undercuts Nirveda and the sales team asks to drop the self-serve price from ₹18,000 to ₹11,000 to win a competitive deal, a 39 percent cut. Gross margin per account falls from ₹10,700 to ₹3,700, a 65 percent drop in margin for a 39 percent drop in price — margin erodes far faster than price because the underlying costs do not move. But the more important change is not the arithmetic; it is what ₹11,000 now tells the next fifty prospects who see it on a public pricing page or hear about it from a peer who negotiated it: that Nirveda's ₹18,000 was never a real price, only an opening bid, and every future buyer will now anchor to ₹11,000 and negotiate down from there. The signal, once broadcast, cannot be selectively withdrawn.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

A price signal is not the same as a fair price

Fairness is about whether a price feels justified relative to cost or to what other customers pay; signalling is about what the price implies regardless of justification. A price can be perfectly fair by cost accounting and still send the wrong signal — Nirveda's usage-based price was arguably the fairest, tying payment to value delivered, and it was also the one most likely to convince an enterprise buyer that Nirveda did not trust its own product enough to charge a flat rate for it.

The signal is carried by the whole price architecture, not the headline number alone

Discount depth, contract length, whether a demo is public or gated behind a sales call, whether the price page exists at all — each of these is a signal in its own right, and buyers read them together. A company with a ₹65,000 headline price that routinely closes at ₹40,000 after negotiation is, in effect, running a ₹40,000 price with a confusing ₹65,000 label on it.

Signals only work when they are costly to fake

Spence's original insight was that a signal is credible only if a low-quality seller could not cheaply imitate it. A high price is a weak signal on its own — anyone can type a large number into a pricing page — which is why credible price signals are usually bundled with something that would be expensive to offer without real quality behind it: a named support team, an uptime guarantee with a financial penalty, a reference customer willing to be named. Price alone, unaccompanied by any of these, signals very little.

A price signal tells you nothing about willingness-to-pay

Knowing what a price implies about positioning is a separate question from knowing what a customer will actually pay, and the two are often confused in pricing workshops. Willingness-to-pay is measured through research — conjoint studies, Van Westendorp surveys, win-loss interviews — while signalling is inferred from how the market reads a number once it is public. A price can send exactly the right signal and still be unaffordable for the segment it targets; signalling and affordability must be checked separately.

It applies differently before and after product-market fit

Before a company has established what its product reliably does for whom, a price signal has very little supporting evidence to draw credibility from, and buyers will discount it heavily; the honest move at that stage is often a lower, more tentative price precisely because the company cannot yet back up a confident one. After fit is established, the same low price becomes a liability, because it now signals a lack of confidence the company has, in fact, earned.

It is routinely confused with premium pricing as a strategy

Charging more is not the same as signalling well; it is possible to signal quality clearly at a low price (a well-designed freemium tier that is honest about its limits) and to signal confusion at a high one (an enterprise price with no enterprise-grade proof points behind it). The nuance is congruence between price and evidence, not the direction of the number.

The signal degrades with every unprincipled exception

Each one-off discount granted to close a deal is invisible to the market until it isn't — sales teams talk, procurement benchmarks circulate, and a pattern of quiet exceptions eventually becomes the real, informally known price, at which point the listed price stops signalling anything at all.

The right diagnostic question is always about inference, not preference

A thoughtful newcomer should not ask "do customers like this price" but "what does a customer who has never spoken to us conclude about who we are, purely from this number, before we say a word." That question, asked honestly, is usually the fastest way to catch a signal that has drifted from what the company actually is.

6. How the signal changes across contexts

In consumer products, the price signal is read almost entirely by the individual paying it, in seconds, often against a shelf of visible substitutes — which is why consumer pricing leans so heavily on charm pricing, tier names, and packaging design to do the signalling work, since there is no salesperson present to reinforce it. In B2B products like Nirveda's, the signal is read by several people in sequence — a user, a finance approver, sometimes a security reviewer — and each reads it slightly differently: the finance approver reads it as a budget-line signal about how seriously to scrutinise the purchase, while the technical user reads a low price as a signal about how much engineering rigour went into the product. In marketplace products, the pricing signal is doubled, because both sides of the marketplace are reading it: a low take-rate signals confidence to sellers that the platform does not need to extract heavily, while the price a buyer pays signals the quality of inventory the platform curates, and the two signals must not contradict each other or one side of the market will infer the platform is favouring the other.

The signal also changes with company age. An early-stage company like Nirveda is signalling largely on potential — its price is read as a bet on where the company is headed, and a slightly aggressive price can be a legitimate way to signal ambition, provided the founders are prepared to defend it in every sales call rather than discount it away. A large, established company's price signals stability and category leadership by default, simply because it has survived; its risk runs the opposite direction; from complacency, where a price that once signalled leadership quietly comes to signal being overpriced and out of touch as newer entrants redefine the category's reference price.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: setting price purely from a cost-plus calculation. The symptom is a pricing memo that opens with "our costs are X, so we need Y percent margin" and never mentions the customer. The underlying misunderstanding is treating price as an internal accounting output rather than an external message. The cheapest diagnostic: ask five customers, without mentioning your number, what they would guess your product costs, and compare their guesses to your plan.

Mistake two: letting the sales team's discount authority silently become the real price. The symptom is a listed price that almost no one actually pays. The underlying misunderstanding is believing that a discount is a private concession rather than a public signal that eventually reaches every future buyer. The cheapest diagnostic: pull the last twenty closed-won deals and check the standard deviation of the effective price paid; a wide spread means the listed price has stopped signalling anything.

Mistake three: changing the price without changing anything else. The symptom is a price increase or cut that moves the number on the page while the sales script, the onboarding experience, and the support model stay identical. The underlying misunderstanding is treating price as an isolated lever rather than one instrument in an ensemble that must stay in tune together. The cheapest diagnostic: after any price change, ask new customers within thirty days what kind of company they thought they were buying from, and see whether the answer matches the new number's intent.

Mistake four: assuming a competitor's price is the correct reference price. The symptom is pricing decisions justified almost entirely by what a named rival charges. The underlying misunderstanding is forgetting that the competitor's price is also a signal, shaped by their own cost structure, ambitions, and history, not a neutral fact about the market. The cheapest diagnostic: ask what would have to be true about your own product, costs, and customers for that competitor's number to also be correct for you — and check whether it actually is.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well, at a company one stage ahead of Nirveda: a Hyderabad-based workflow-automation firm, three years old, that had gone through this exact tension with its own enterprise tier. Its product leadership had resisted a usage-based enterprise price, despite its analytical appeal, until they could show, account by account, that a typical enterprise customer's usage would keep gross margin above sixty percent even in a slow month — the same test the Nirveda table above ought to pass before any number leaves a whiteboard. They had also refused to let the sales team discount the enterprise tier by more than eight percent without a product-leadership sign-off, precisely because they understood that every unauthorised exception was quietly rewriting their price signal for the next negotiation. And when they did raise the self-serve tier's price by twenty percent, they did it in the same release that added a service-level guarantee with a financial penalty attached, so the new number arrived already backed by evidence rather than asking the market to take it on faith. The result was not a single clever price but a set of numbers that agreed with each other, with the product's real cost structure, and with what each tier's customers were told to expect — the definition of a signal that holds up under scrutiny.

Figure 2. A price signal holds only when the number, the supporting evidence, and the underlying cost to serve all point the same direction; break any one leg and the market stops trusting the price to mean anything.

9. What Meera decided, and where to go next

Meera went into the board meeting with the enterprise number, ₹65,000 a month with a named customer-success manager, but not as a blanket replacement for the self-serve tier — as a second, explicit tier sitting above it, with the self-serve ₹18,000 tier kept for the mid-market base it already fit and clearly labelled as self-serve, no dedicated support, so its lower price stopped looking like an accident and started looking like a deliberate promise. She shelved the usage-based formula, not because it was a bad idea in principle but because Nirveda's accounts were not yet large enough for the arithmetic to hold, and she told Arvind she would revisit it once average screened volume per account crossed roughly ₹30 crore a month, the rough point at which the earlier table's margin turned positive. Her reasoning, stated in the board deck, was the sentence from section two: the price is the clearest claim the company makes about who it is for, and Nirveda needed two claims, not one blurred compromise, because it was now serving two real kinds of customer with genuinely different needs.

What Meera has learned next, and what any reader of this page should learn next, is how to test willingness-to-pay directly rather than inferring it from signalling logic alone — through structured customer interviews and instruments like the Van Westendorp price-sensitivity survey — because signalling tells you what a price implies, not what a segment can actually afford, and a company needs both answers before it can be confident in a number. It is also worth studying how the same congruence logic scales to AI-native products, where the inference cost per user is far less stable than Nirveda's, and where a usage-based price is often the only one that keeps gross margin honest as model calls grow — the exact tension Meera set aside for later, not because it was wrong, but because Nirveda was not yet the company that number described.

Our price is the clearest claim we make about who we built this for — read before a single feature is.

Two questions worth sitting with. First: if a prospect who has never spoken to your company saw only your price, with every feature list and testimonial hidden, what would they conclude about who you built the product for — and is that the customer you actually want? Second: pull your last quarter's closed deals and look at the spread between your listed price and what customers actually paid; if that spread is wide, what is your price actually signalling now, and to whom?

Ajasra Cold-Press Foods: The Shelf Price Question

A decision case on what a price says about who a brand is for

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 7 October 2026, Aarti Maheshwari sat in her office above the pressing hall in Latur and read the same email for the fourth time. It came from the category buyer of a national supermarket chain that had stocked Ajasra Cold-Press Foods for two years. The chain's listing review was on 15 October. The buyer wanted Ajasra's one-litre cold-pressed groundnut oil, printed at ₹630, on the shelf at ₹525 before Diwali on 8 November. In return, the chain would more than double the number of stores carrying it.

Aarti, the founder and chief executive, had until Friday, 9 October to reply. Her team disagreed, and the question was not only about margin but about what the number on the bottle told a shopper about who Ajasra was for.

2. Company background

Ajasra was founded in 2017 by Aarti, a food technologist. She had watched farmers in Beed and Dharashiv sell groundnut, sesame and safflower seed to large crushers while others captured the value of the oil. Ajasra began with one slow-speed press in Latur and now has a second pressing hall in Nanded, opened in 2023, and a collection centre in Akola for sesame and safflower. The press date is printed on every label.

The company sells four ways: its own website and app with subscriptions (direct to consumer, or D2C), quick-commerce platforms such as Zepto and Blinkit, modern-trade supermarkets, and a small export line through an importer in Rotterdam and a distributor in Colombo. Groundnut oil is the anchor. Edible oil carries 5 per cent GST, and labelling follows FSSAI rules.

At the bottom sit mass refined oils from brands such as Fortune and Saffola. Above them are branded filtered groundnut oils, including Tata Sampann and regional brands, and above these other premium cold-pressed labels. Figure 1 places Ajasra on this ladder.

6. The options

Option A: match the chain at ₹525. The upside is volume and a safe relationship. The cost is severe: contribution per bottle falls from ₹86 to ₹10, the D2C price looks inflated, and net contribution turns negative by ₹15.6 lakh.

Option B: hold ₹630 and decline. The upside is a price that keeps saying premium to shoppers, subscribers and export partners, and a margin that funds the quality proof. The cost is a smaller footprint, a possible delisting, and ₹68.8 lakh less contribution.

The upside is a lower first-purchase price with the price per litre unchanged, and a new item at a visibly lower shelf price for Diwali. The cost is complexity, a small one-off spend and dependence on a buyer who has not yet been asked.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Figure 1, what does ₹525 say about Ajasra to a new shopper? Who does ₹630 say it is for?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, why is the same bottle worth less to Ajasra in modern trade than in D2C, and which channel should set the price?
  3. Which assumptions in Exhibit 3 would you challenge first, and how far must they move for Option A to beat Option C?
  4. What would you write to the buyer on 9 October, and what would you tell Anouk Visser and Ruwan Fernando?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision through one idea: price communicates positioning. A price is the first thing a customer reads about quality and about who the product is for. Ajasra's difficulty is that one product is read at several prices at once: a shopper on the shelf, a subscriber on the app and a buyer in Rotterdam each compare the numbers they see. A local cut becomes a signal to all of them.

A well-reasoned answer separates two things the request blurs: the price per litre, which carries the premium message, and the price of a first purchase, which sets how easy it is to try the brand. Option A moves the first and pays in every channel, as Exhibit 3 shows. Option B protects it but ignores the buyer's real problem: shoppers reluctant to commit ₹630 to an unfamiliar bottle.

The defensible path is Option C. Ajasra keeps ₹630 a litre, offers the chain the 500 ml bottle at ₹315 as a Diwali item, and explains it in terms of her stores: a lower entry price with the same quality signal. The ₹36 contribution a bottle is 15.8 per cent of net, against 2.6 per cent for the discounted litre. It improves annual contribution by ₹10.6 lakh after the one-off cost, and does not disturb Rotterdam or Colombo. Safeguards: a review after the first quarter, and identical labels on both sizes, so the small bottle reads as the same product, not a cheaper one. If the buyer refuses, Ajasra should accept a smaller listing under Option B rather than move to ₹525, because a price, once lowered, is very hard to raise.

What Pricing Signals

A price is a claim about identity. A claim is worth only what it would cost to make falsely.

This reading assumes the working treatment of price signalling: that a price carries information about quality and intended buyer, that buyers read it against a reference price, that congruence between the number and every other cue matters, and that discounting broadcasts. It starts where that account stops — with the question of what actually makes a price credible, what the formal treatment says about when it is not, and what experienced operators do about the fact that the signal is set in six places by five departments and owned by none of them.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On the morning of 6 October 2026, Devika Nambiar, chief product officer of Amritvela Systems, stood on a mezzanine walkway above an auto-component plant near Chakan, outside Pune, and watched one of her company's inspection units fail to be interesting. The unit — a camera bar and an edge compute box mounted over a machining line, running a defect-detection model trained on the customer's own scrap history — had been catching burr and porosity defects at a recall the plant's quality head measured at ninety-six percent over eleven weeks. It had paid for itself. The plant head liked it. And the purchase had taken eight and a half months to close, because Amritvela had priced the hardware at ₹6.8 lakh per line, which in this customer's approval architecture made it a capital item, and capital items went to a committee that met in February and August.

Devika's problem, which she would put to her CFO Arun Pillai and her sales head Harpreet Sethi the following week, was not that ₹6.8 lakh was too much money. Over three years, at four lines, the customer would spend something close to ₹56 lakh on Amritvela either way, and the return on scrap reduction alone was a little over ₹1.1 crore. The problem was that the shape of the price had put the decision in front of the wrong committee, and that everything about the committee's mental model — depreciation schedules, vendor financial strength, comparison against imported inspection rigs from established European instrumentation firms — read Amritvela as a small capital-equipment supplier rather than as what it believed itself to be, which was a software company with a sensor attached. The number had made a claim about identity, and it was the wrong claim. Devika had four alternative configurations on a single sheet of paper, and by the end of the month she had to choose one, because the channel partners who would carry Amritvela into the Coimbatore and Rajkot clusters in 2027 needed a price list they could publish.

Four hundred kilometres to the south and six weeks later, on 18 November 2026, Zoya Kher was arguing with her own unit economics. Kher had co-founded Amiya Learning in 2023 with Nikhil Bose; the product was a speech-to-speech English and interview-preparation coach that learners spoke to on their phones, mostly in the evenings, mostly in tier-two cities, mostly between the ages of nineteen and twenty-six. It had 1.9 lakh monthly active users on a free tier and 4,560 paying subscribers at ₹499 a month. The free tier was the growth engine and it was also, as Bose had been pointing out since June, a ₹1.16 crore monthly bill for inference against ₹22.8 lakh of monthly subscription revenue. Amiya had raised money on that trade; investors had bought the story. The question in front of Kher was the proposed third tier — a placement-preparation product at ₹2,400 a month that bundled two live human mock interviews with a trained coach — and whether a company whose entire public identity had been built on ₹499 could ask for 4.8 times that number without the market concluding one of two unhelpful things: that the ₹499 product had always been a stripped-down tease, or that the ₹2,400 product was a cynical upsell with an app behind it.

Kher's growth lead, Tara D'Souza, framed the disagreement precisely in a Monday review: "Against every other app on a learner's phone, ₹2,400 a month is absurd. Against the offline placement coaching in Vijayawada or Indore that these same learners' families are already paying ₹28,000 for, it is a bargain. We are not choosing a price. We are choosing which of those two shelves the buyer thinks they are standing in front of." That is the sharpest available statement of what this reading is about, and it points at the thing the working treatment of price signalling tends to leave unexamined: the buyer's reference class is not a fact about the market, it is partly a variable the seller controls, and a great deal of expert practice consists of moving it.

Hold both scenes. Devika is choosing the shape of a price in a way that determines which human being inside a customer organisation reads it. Kher is choosing the reference class against which a number is read. Neither is choosing a level, which is what most pricing conversations think they are about. The argument of this page is that they are both doing the same thing, that this thing is more fundamental than level-setting, and that it has a formal structure with a testable threshold — one that tells you, quantitatively, when your price is capable of signalling anything at all and when it is merely a number you are hoping people believe.

2. The idea, more precisely than before

Define the term tightly. A price signal is an inference a buyer draws about unobservable product attributes — quality, intended segment, the seller's own confidence, the likely durability of the relationship — from the observable price, in a situation where the buyer cannot verify those attributes before committing. The inference is not about the money. It is about what the seller's willingness to name that number reveals, given that the seller knows things the buyer does not.

The intellectual lineage runs through three distinct literatures that are routinely blurred together, and separating them is the first move that distinguishes an expert. The first is signalling theory proper, from Michael Spence's 1973 work on job-market signalling. Spence's contribution was not the observation that people use proxies; that is ancient. It was the equilibrium condition: a signal conveys information only when the cost of sending it differs by type, so that a low-quality sender finds imitation unprofitable. A degree signals ability not because education is valuable but because it is cheaper to obtain for the able. Applied to price, the proposition is uncomfortable: a high price on its own is almost free to imitate — typing a larger number into a pricing page costs nothing — and therefore, on Spence's own logic, a bare price should signal nothing. The 1986 extension by Paul Milgrom and John Roberts closed this gap by showing that price can signal quality in equilibrium when it is bundled with a repeat-purchase structure or with dissipative expenditure such as advertising: the high-quality firm is willing to sacrifice first-period margin because it expects to be around for the second period, and the low-quality firm is not.

The second literature is price–quality inference in marketing and psychology, associated with Kent Monroe from the 1970s onward and later with Akshay Rao and Kent Monroe's meta-analytic work. This tradition asks an empirical rather than a theoretical question: do buyers infer quality from price, and how much? The answer that emerged is more equivocal than the folklore suggests. Published meta-analyses of objective quality ratings against price across consumer categories have found average correlations in the region of 0.25 to 0.30, with wide dispersion and near-zero or negative correlations in many individual product classes. The inference is real but weak in aggregate, and it strengthens sharply in exactly the conditions Spence's model would predict: high perceived risk, low search possibility, infrequent purchase, no accessible third-party evaluation.

The third is reference-price theory, running from Helson's adaptation-level psychology through Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory to Russell Winer's work on reference prices in brand choice and Richard Thaler's concept of transaction utility. Its claim is that buyers do not evaluate prices absolutely at all; they evaluate the gap between the observed price and an internal reference, and they are loss-averse about that gap. This matters because it makes the price signal a relative object. Amiya's ₹2,400 has no signal value in itself. It has one value against the reference class of mobile applications and a different one against the reference class of coaching institutes.

The schools, and the propositions each will and will not sign

Four positions are held by serious people. It is worth stating what each would actually put its name to, because practitioners argue past each other by assuming the disagreement is about emphasis when it is about mechanism.

The signalling school will sign: "under information asymmetry, price is one of the few costly, public, hard-to-hedge statements a seller makes, and a price incongruent with the seller's other commitments will be discounted by sophisticated buyers." It will not sign: "raising price raises perceived quality." It regards that as the naïve corruption of its own idea, because a price rise unaccompanied by a change in the cost of imitation changes nothing about the equilibrium.

The value-based pricing school — Thomas Nagle and Reed Holden's framework, and in contemporary product management Madhavan Ramanujam's argument for willingness-to-pay conversations before a feature is built — will sign: "price should be derived from quantified economic value to the customer, segment by segment, and the shape of the offer should be designed around what customers will pay for." It will not sign the proposition that the signal should ever distort the number. In this school signalling is a communication problem solved downstream by packaging, naming and proof, and a firm that sets its price to send a message has simply failed to do the value analysis.

The behavioural / reference-price school will sign: "the level is nearly irrelevant; the perceived gap from the reference and the framing of the unit are what move behaviour, and a seller who cannot state the buyer's reference price does not know their own price." It will not sign the signalling school's implicit rationality: it holds that buyers' inferences are frequently wrong, manipulable, and unstable across framings, and it is therefore sceptical of any theory that treats price inference as informationally efficient.

The unit-economics school, which has grown loud in the past three years because of the cost structure of AI products, will sign: "price is an output of a cost-to-serve model and a gross-margin commitment, and a value metric that does not track the dominant marginal cost is a time bomb." It will not sign the proposition that signalling should ever override margin. Its practitioners have watched companies hold a confident flat price while variable inference cost ate the business from below, and they regard signalling arguments in that setting as an expensive form of vanity.

The synthesis usually offered — "of course you need all four" — is not held by anyone who has to make the decision, because the four schools prescribe different actions when they conflict, and they conflict constantly. Devika's choice between capital and operating expenditure is a case where the value school and the signalling school give the same answer and the behavioural school gives a different one. Kher's choice is a case where the unit-economics school and the signalling school point in opposite directions for the free tier. The honest position is that you must know which school you are following on each decision and why.

3. Mechanics in depth: what makes a price credible

The mechanism worth internalising is not the four-step chain of reference price, comparison, congruence and broadcast. That chain describes what happens to a signal. It does not tell you whether you have one. The deeper question is the Spence question: what would it cost an inferior competitor to make the same claim? If the answer is "nothing", the claim carries no information, and no amount of congruent branding will make it carry information — it will only make the bluff more convincing for longer, which is a different and more dangerous thing.

Work this through with Amritvela's actual numbers, because the arithmetic is unexpectedly decisive and most practitioners have never done it.

Amritvela's software subscription lists at ₹2.40 lakh per inspection line per year. The company's cost to serve a line is ₹0.38 lakh of edge and cloud compute plus ₹0.52 lakh of field engineering and quarterly model retuning — ₹0.90 lakh, giving a gross margin of ₹1.50 lakh, or 62.5 percent. Observed annual retention across its 2024–2026 cohort is 88 percent. At a 14 percent cost of capital, the present value of the margin stream from one line is ₹1.50 lakh divided by (0.14 + 0.12), the sum of discount rate and churn rate — ₹5.77 lakh.

Now model the imitator. Suppose a competitor assembles an off-the-shelf industrial camera with a generic pretrained defect model, no customer-specific tuning, no field engineering. Its cost to serve is ₹0.35 lakh a year. If it prices honestly at what such a product is worth — call it ₹0.95 lakh, which is roughly where the commodity end of the Indian machine-vision market sat in 2026 — it earns ₹0.60 lakh a year at, say, 70 percent retention, for a present value of ₹0.60 / (0.14 + 0.30) = ₹1.36 lakh. If instead it mimics Amritvela's ₹2.40 lakh price, it earns ₹2.05 lakh in year one and then loses the customer entirely, for a present value of roughly ₹2.05 / (0.14 + 1.00) = ₹1.80 lakh.

Mimicry pays. ₹1.80 lakh beats ₹1.36 lakh. Amritvela's high price is not self-enforcing: in the language of the model, there is no separating equilibrium, and a buyer who understands this — and procurement departments at large Indian manufacturers understand it in their bones even if they have never seen the algebra — is correct to treat the ₹2.40 lakh as uninformative. This is the single most important result on this page. Most premium prices in most B2B software categories fail this test. The gap between one year of inflated margin and the discounted value of an honest commodity business is simply not large enough to deter imitation, because software churn punishment is slow, referenceability is opaque, and most buyers cannot tell in year one whether they bought quality.

Figure 1. Amritvela's premium price only deters imitation if a bad product is detected and punished almost immediately. In industrial software, where a poor deployment can be blamed on the customer's data for three quarters, detection is slow — so the price alone carries no information. The remedy is not a different price; it is an added commitment that is expensive for a poor seller and cheap for a good one.

Restoring the equilibrium: the arithmetic of a guarantee

What restores separation is a commitment whose expected cost depends on quality. Suppose Amritvela publishes, in its standard contract and on its public price list, a service credit: if measured recall against the customer's own scrap audit falls below 95 percent in any quarter, the customer receives a credit of ₹X for that quarter. Amritvela's own observed breach rate across its installed base is about 7 percent of quarters, or 0.28 quarters a year. The imitator, running an untuned generic model, would breach in roughly 85 percent of quarters, or 3.4 quarters a year.

The deterrence condition is that the guarantee must cost the imitator more, in present value, than its gain from mimicry over honest pricing — that is, more than ₹1.80 − ₹1.36 = ₹0.44 lakh. The imitator's expected first-year payout is 3.4X; discounted, about 3.18X. Setting 3.18X > 0.44 gives X > ₹0.138 lakh, or roughly ₹14,000 a quarter. Amritvela's own expected annual cost is 0.28 × ₹14,000 ≈ ₹3,900, which reduces the present value of a line from ₹5.77 lakh to about ₹5.75 lakh. A commitment that costs the honest seller four thousand rupees a year destroys the imitator's entire business case. That is a price signal. The ₹2.40 lakh was never the signal; it was the headline on one.

Two second-order effects follow immediately, and they are where the expert lives. First, real firms set guarantees five to ten times larger than the deterrence threshold, and the naïve reading is that they are being generous or badly advised. The correct reading is that buyers discount guarantees by the probability that they will actually be honoured — a credit that requires a dispute, a legal notice and a renewal negotiation to collect is worth a fraction of its face value — so the seller must overshoot to clear the threshold after the buyer's own haircut. The observable tell is whether the guarantee is self-executing (automatic credit on a metered condition) or claimable (customer must raise a ticket). Self-executing guarantees can be small; claimable ones must be large.

Second, the guarantee changes who inside the customer can approve the purchase, which is the mechanism Devika actually needed. A quality head who has a contractual recall floor with a rupee number attached can defend the purchase to a plant director without invoking faith. The commitment is not only a signal to the market; it is an internal instrument the buyer's champion uses to win an argument you are not present for. Experienced pricing people design for that argument explicitly.

The dispersion measure: what the market actually hears

The second quantitative object worth carrying is the distribution of realised prices. A list price is a claim; the realised distribution is the evidence. Amritvela's 2026 closed-won book showed a mean realised subscription of ₹2.09 lakh against a ₹2.40 lakh list, with a standard deviation of ₹0.46 lakh — a coefficient of variation of 0.22. A serviceable rule of thumb, derived from nothing more rigorous than the point at which buyers begin opening negotiations at numbers the seller has never published, is that above a coefficient of variation of about 0.25 the list price stops functioning as information and becomes an opening bid. Below about 0.12 the list price is effectively the price and the signal is clean.

The related arithmetic that deal desks should have laminated: a discount of d percentage points on a product with gross margin m requires a volume increase of d ⁄ (m − d) to hold gross profit constant. At Amritvela's 62.5 percent margin, a 20 percent discount needs 47 percent more volume; a 30 percent discount needs 92 percent more. Sales leaders asked to defend a discount in these terms rather than in terms of "winning the logo" produce visibly better arguments, and the ones who cannot produce the argument usually stop asking.

4. When the idea applies, and when it actively misleads

State the conditions as claims that can be checked, and apply each to both protagonists. The discipline of testing rather than asserting is most of what separates a pricing decision from a pricing opinion.

Where is the idea actively misleading rather than merely inapplicable? Three situations recur. The first is commodity categories with transparent specification, where the buyer can verify quality precisely and cheaply — cloud storage per gigabyte, payment gateway basis points, bulk SMS. Here a high price signals nothing except that you have not read the market, and reasoning about "premium positioning" produces companies that lose on price while explaining to themselves that they are differentiated.

The second is categories with strong third-party verification. When an accreditation body, a rating platform or a regulator collapses the information asymmetry, price inference weakens sharply because the buyer no longer needs it. A NABL-accredited pathology lab and an unaccredited one are distinguishable without looking at the price list; the accreditation has done the signalling work, and the price is free to do something else — which is precisely why accredited chains compete hard on price for routine panels without being read as low quality.

The third, and the most costly in practice, is when the buyer's true constraint is budget authority rather than value perception. This was Amritvela's actual situation, and the reason its pricing debate had been unproductive for two quarters. The company had been arguing about whether ₹6.8 lakh signalled seriousness or extravagance while the operative fact was that ₹6.8 lakh crossed a capital-approval threshold and ₹4.0 lakh did not. Signalling logic applied to an authority problem produces elegant reasoning about the wrong variable. The diagnostic is simple and underused: ask the champion, "who signs this, and what is the number above which someone else signs it?" If the deal moves when the number crosses an approval line and does not move when it crosses a value line, you have an authority problem wearing a signalling costume.

The mitigation is that the company surveyed nineteen target accounts and found capital thresholds clustered at ₹3, ₹5 and ₹10 lakh, with ₹4 lakh clearing a majority — a real piece of market research that most companies never do and that is far more decisive than another week of willingness-to-pay debate.

Two-sided platforms: one number, two audiences, opposite readings

Amaravati Freight Exchange, a Hyderabad-based digital load exchange matching shippers with fleet owners across the southern and western corridors, ran a take rate of 7.5 percent on roughly ₹96 crore of monthly gross booking value — about ₹7.2 crore of monthly revenue. In August 2026 its head of marketplace, Srikanth Vemuri, faced a competitive proposal to cut the take rate to 5 percent, which would surrender ₹2.4 crore a month in exchange for supply-side growth.

The signalling analysis is genuinely two-sided and the two readings run in opposite directions. To fleet owners, a lower take rate signals a platform that does not need to extract, which reads as confidence and generosity — a good signal. To shippers, the same cut signals something else entirely: that the platform's margin no longer supports the verification work — permit checks, insurance validity, driver antecedents, GPS compliance — that is the only reason a shipper uses an exchange rather than the broker they have used for fifteen years. A shipper who reads a take-rate cut as thinning verification will not say so; they will simply route their high-value consignments through the broker and their low-value ones through the platform, and the exchange will find its average consignment value declining without a single complaint.

The expert move on two-sided platforms is to separate the take rate into a matching fee and a verification fee, so that a cut can be aimed at one side's reading without being received by the other. Amaravati eventually went to 5.0 percent matching plus a 1.5 percent verification charge borne by the shipper and visible as a line item, with the verification standard published. Supply-side perception improved; shipper-side perception improved more, because for the first time the thing they were paying for had a name.

Regulated markets: when disclosure flattens the signal

Prerna Sanghvi runs product for Amritkosh Money, a Mumbai lending platform. Since the Reserve Bank of India's key-fact-statement requirements made the all-in annual percentage rate mandatory, comparable and prominent, the price of a personal loan has become one of the most transparent numbers in Indian retail finance. Amritkosh's 16.4 percent APR sits in a visible field of 15.8 to 22 percent.

Mandated disclosure does not remove price signalling; it relocates it. When the headline price is standardised, differentiation migrates to the terms that are not standardised — disbursal time, prepayment charges, the conduct of collections, whether a top-up is pre-approved. Sanghvi's observation, after eighteen months of experiments, was that Amritkosh's most informative price signal had become its processing fee: at 1.25 percent against a market norm above 2 percent, it was the one number that a borrower read as a statement about whether the lender was trying to extract at the moment of maximum information asymmetry, which is the five minutes before signing. Regulated categories reward practitioners who can find the unregulated margin of the price architecture and make it carry the claim. They punish those who conclude that because the headline is fixed, pricing is no longer a product decision.

Multi-product lines: the loudest price is the cheapest visible one

Amsara Diagnostics Network, an Ahmedabad pathology chain, runs a menu of 340 tests from a ₹390 lipid profile to a ₹4,800 executive panel. Dr. Ila Trivedi, who runs its consumer business, found in 2026 that patients' perception of Amsara's overall price level correlated almost entirely with the price of the two or three routine tests they had purchased before — the complete blood count, the thyroid panel — and not at all with the price of the panels that generated most of the margin. The cheapest visible price in a multi-product line sets the perceived price of the whole line, which means a promotional discount on a routine test is not a promotion; it is a permanent revision of the brand's price signal, paid for out of a budget line called marketing.

AI-native products: the signal attacked from below

Amitava Contracts Cloud, a Kolkata company selling contract review to legal teams, priced at ₹180 per document reviewed when it launched in mid-2025, against an inference cost of ₹94 — a 48 percent gross margin that its founder Rudra Sen defended as a confident, value-anchored number. By late 2026 the same review ran at ₹21 of inference. The margin had gone to 88 percent without a single product improvement, and a competitor had launched at ₹60.

Two things happen to a price signal when the marginal cost underneath it collapses. The first is that the price stops being read as a claim about quality and starts being read as a claim about the seller's intentions: a buyer who knows model costs have fallen by seventy-five percent and sees your price unchanged concludes not that you are premium but that you are extracting. The second is subtler and more damaging. A per-unit price is an implicit promise that the unit is comparable; when the cost of producing the unit falls by a factor of four, competitors flood in at the new cost floor and the unit becomes a commodity — at which point the seller who is genuinely better must re-express their price in a metric that is not the commodity. Amitava's eventual move was to price per reviewed contract value at risk rather than per document, a metric that tracked the buyer's exposure rather than the seller's compute, and to publish a liability-backed accuracy commitment. Whether that survives contact with a general-purpose model that does the same job inside a productivity suite is, honestly, unknown.

The organisational seam: who actually sets the price

Ask a company what its price is and you will be told a list price. Ask the market and you will be told a distribution. Between the two sit six separate decisions, owned by five functions, none of which is accountable for the coherence of the result.

The distribution below — including the long left tail contributed by channel partners, who discount to protect their own margin — is the signal the market receives. Mature companies do not manage the list price; they manage the width of that distribution.

What mature companies say they do is value-based pricing. What they actually do, on inspection, is run a floor-price table, a monthly exception log and a quarterly review of realised-price dispersion by segment — and the floor, not the list, is the real price. The gap between the stated practice and the actual practice is not hypocrisy; the floor table is the more sophisticated instrument, because it is the one that controls the signal. The failure is that the floor is usually owned by sales operations and never shown to product, so the company's public identity is being set weekly by a spreadsheet nobody in product management has read.

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the reference class is chosen, not given — and choosing it is most of the job. A competent practitioner researches what competitors charge. An expert first establishes, empirically, what the buyer spontaneously compares against, and then asks whether that comparison set can be moved. The tell in the wild is a seller who has instrumented the question: they can tell you that in nineteen discovery calls, eleven prospects compared them to headcount and eight to a named product, and they price and pitch differently to each. The obvious reading — that the reference class is a market fact to be discovered — is wrong because the comparison a buyer makes is heavily determined by the frame the seller opens with. Amiya's ₹2,400 is either five times an app or a tenth of a coaching course depending on the first sentence of the landing page.

Two: the person who reads the price is rarely the person who uses the product, and the gap widens with organisation size. A price must be dual-coded: legible as value to the user and as risk to the approver. The tell is a company whose sales cycles die not at "we don't like it" but at "we love it, and finance asked what this actually is." The obvious reading is that this is a sales-enablement problem. It is usually a price-architecture problem: the number is expressed in a unit the user manages and the approver cannot audit. Amritvela's per-line subscription was legible to a plant head because lines are a thing a plant head counts; a per-inspection price would have been unauditable and would have been declined.

Three: credibility is stored in the dispersion, not in the level. An expert watches the standard deviation of realised price with more attention than the mean. The tell is what happens at the start of a negotiation: if procurement opens at a number you have never published, your dispersion has leaked and your list price has already stopped signalling. The obvious reading — that a wide spread simply means flexible pricing — is wrong because flexibility that cannot be explained by a published rule is indistinguishable, from the buyer's side, from a list price that was never real.

Four: unit framing changes the signal without changing the money. ₹2,88,000 a year, ₹24,000 a month and ₹790 a day are the same cash and three different claims — the first about a budget commitment, the second about an operating expense, the third about triviality. The tell is an internal argument about "how to display the price" that is conducted as a design question. It is not a design question; it is a positioning decision being made by whoever owns the pricing page. The obvious reading, that buyers do the division, is wrong: they do the division and still respond to the frame, which is one of the better-replicated findings in the behavioural literature.

Five: the free tier is a price, and often the most-read one. Every limit on a free plan is a statement about what the company believes is valuable and who it thinks is not worth serving. The tell of an expert is a free tier whose limits are expressed in the unit that actually drives the company's cost — Amiya's free tier capped at ten conversations, which correlated poorly with inference minutes, so a small number of very long conversations consumed a disproportionate share of a ₹1.16 crore monthly bill. The obvious reading is that free-tier limits are a conversion-optimisation problem. They are simultaneously a cost-control instrument and a signal, and optimising for conversion alone reliably produces limits that are generous in exactly the dimension that is expensive.

Six: price changes signal more than price levels. The first derivative carries information the level cannot. A company that has held the same price for four years signals to sophisticated buyers and to investors that it has added nothing worth charging for, which is often true. A company that raises price annually by a modest amount alongside a published change log signals a product under active investment. The tell is whether renewal quotes are identical to three years ago. The obvious reading — that holding price is customer-friendly — is wrong in B2B, where the procurement function expects annual uplift, budgets for it, and treats its absence as a sign of a vendor in trouble.

Seven: the signal is set as much by who you refuse as by what you charge. An expert kills deals to protect the number, and can name the last three they killed. This is the costly-to-fake condition operating at the level of sales behaviour rather than contract terms: a company that walks away from a ₹40 lakh deal because the buyer would not accept the floor has made a statement that a bluffing competitor cannot cheaply imitate, and the statement travels through the same procurement networks that carry discount gossip. The obvious reading is that walking away is a luxury for companies with full pipelines. In practice it is most valuable for companies with thin pipelines, because they are the ones whose price is least believed.

Eight: discounts on term and volume preserve the signal; discounts on pleading destroy it. The operational test is beautifully simple — could you publish your discount table? A schedule that says "three-year prepaid, minus 12 percent; above eight lines, minus 9 percent" can be published, and publishing it converts a concession into a rule, which is to say into information. A schedule that in practice reads "whatever the regional manager needs in the last week of the quarter" cannot be published, and the reason it cannot be published is precisely the reason it destroys the signal. The tell is quarter-end seasonality in realised price: if your discount distribution has a fat tail in the last ten days of each quarter, your buyers have already learnt to wait.

Nine: in AI products the signal is attacked from below by falling marginal cost and from above by output variance. Falling inference cost erodes the defensibility of any per-unit price; output variance erodes the credibility of any confident price, because a premium price is an implicit reliability claim that a stochastic system may not keep. The tell of an expert working on an AI product is that their pricing discussion keeps turning into an evaluation-coverage discussion — what fraction of the output distribution have we actually measured, and can we make a commitment about it? The obvious reading is that these are separate workstreams owned by different teams. They are one workstream: you cannot make a costly-to-fake commitment about behaviour you have not measured, and without such a commitment the price is a bare number.

Ten: signals decay, and the half-life is shorter than anyone plans for. A price that accurately described a company in 2023 describes a different market in 2026 because the reference price has moved underneath it. The tell is a company whose price has not changed while the category's entry price has halved, and whose sales team has begun to describe the price as "something we have to get past early in the call." The obvious reading is that this is a competitive-response problem requiring a price cut. Sometimes it is; more often it is a reference-class problem requiring the company to stop being compared to the thing that got cheap, which is a packaging and value-metric decision rather than a level decision.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage — and where it does not

Start with where the differences are not real, because the folklore is full of them. It is commonly said that consumer buyers are more price-signal sensitive than enterprise buyers. The evidence does not support the distinction as stated; the inference mechanism is identical. What differs is the number of readers, the latency of the reading and the availability of substitutes for the inference. A consumer reads a price alone, in three seconds, with reviews and a visible shelf of alternatives that partially substitute for price inference. An enterprise buying committee reads it over eleven months, with four people forming different inferences and a procurement function whose explicit job is to defeat the seller's framing. The enterprise buyer is not less susceptible; they are slower and more adversarial, which changes the tactics entirely and the mechanism not at all.

Where the differences are real, they are these. In consumer subscriptions, the punishment for a bluff arrives in a month — cancellation is one tap — so condition C2 almost never holds and price cannot carry a quality claim on its own. Consumer price signals therefore work almost entirely through relative structure: the presence of a more expensive tier makes the middle tier legible, which is the well-documented compromise effect, and the decoy tier earns its keep even if nobody buys it. Amiya's ₹2,400 tier will make ₹499 feel like a considered choice rather than a cheap one, and that effect is worth having even at low attach.

In B2B and enterprise software, the dominant fact is that the price is read by a committee and then benchmarked by people outside it — peers, analysts, procurement consortia. The signal's durability matters more than its initial force, and the operative discipline is dispersion control. In platforms and marketplaces, the price is a take rate and it is read in opposite directions by the two sides, so the architecture question — how many separately-named fees, and who bears each — dominates the level question, as Amaravati found.

In hardware and physical goods, price carries a manufacturing-cost inference that software does not: buyers have a rough intuition for what metal, optics and assembly cost, and a price far below that intuition reads as corner-cutting rather than efficiency. This is why hardware companies cannot use the software playbook of aggressive introductory pricing without damage. It is also why the capex–opex seam exists at all, and why the shape of a hardware-plus-software price is a governance decision in the buyer's organisation before it is a marketing decision in the seller's.

In AI-native products, the distinguishing fact is that the marginal cost is both large and falling fast, which makes the value metric the load-bearing decision and the level almost a residual. A per-seat price on an AI product signals "this is a tool your people use"; a per-outcome price signals "we are accountable for the result"; a per-token or per-call price signals "we are a utility and you should shop us." Each is a different company. Amitava's migration from per-document to per-contract-value was a change of identity dressed as a change of billing.

8. Three worked examples

Example one: Amritvela reshapes a price without changing the money

Amritvela moved from configuration A to configuration D in January 2027 for new business, holding existing customers on their contracted terms. The three-year customer outlay fell from ₹56.0 lakh to ₹54.2 lakh for a four-line deployment — a 3.2 percent reduction — and Amritvela's three-year gross margin fell from ₹35.8 lakh to ₹34.2 lakh, a 4.5 percent reduction. On those numbers alone the change looks like a mild giveaway. The relevant numbers are elsewhere. Median sales cycle across the next eleven closed deals fell from 8.5 months to 3.9 months, because the decision no longer waited for a capital committee. Working-capital-adjusted, the shorter cycle was worth more than the surrendered margin within the first year. Two of the eleven deals came through channel partners in Coimbatore who, for the first time, had a price list they could quote from without escalation.

The instructive detail is what Amritvela shipped alongside the new price, in the same release: a self-executing quarterly service credit of ₹90,000 per line if measured recall fell below 95 percent against the customer's own scrap audit, credited automatically without a claim. That figure is six times the ₹14,000 deterrence threshold computed in section 3, deliberately, to survive the buyer's own discount for enforceability. It cost Amritvela ₹25,000 across the eleven accounts in the first year. It was mentioned in nine of the eleven deals as a reason for confidence, and in two of them it was the item the quality head used to win an internal argument Devika was not in the room for.

Example two: Amiya splits the reference class

Kher launched the ₹2,400 tier on 1 February 2027, but not as a tier. The insight from D'Souza's Monday remark was carried through completely: the placement product was given its own name, its own landing surface, its own sales motion through campus placement cells, and its price was quoted as ₹2,400 a month against the explicit comparison of an offline placement course at ₹28,000 for four months. On the main app, the two-tier structure of free and ₹499 was preserved unchanged, and the ₹2,400 product was surfaced only to users who had completed more than forty sessions — that is, to users who had already stopped comparing Amiya to other apps.

The brand had built a defensible price signal over three years: a four-times-commodity price backed by farm traceability, small-batch dating, and a refusal to list on discount-heavy channels.

In October 2024, facing a flat quarter and a marketplace-funded festive event, its founder Yash Bhandari agreed to a five-week promotion at ₹399. The mechanics worked spectacularly. Amrai sold 61 percent of its annual unit volume in those five weeks. It also, in the same five weeks, told every customer and every competitor exactly what it thought its product was worth.

9. Failure modes, with their early warning signs

Each of the following has a characteristic early signature, a diagnostic that catches it cheaply, and a cost of catching it late that is disproportionate to the cost of catching it early. The asymmetry is the point: price-signal failures are cheap to detect and expensive to remediate, which is the opposite of most product failures and the reason they are chronically under-monitored.
