The one worth expanding is the last, because it is the most frequently misdiagnosed. When a price signal attracts the wrong segment, the symptom is not a pricing symptom. It appears eighteen to twenty-four months later as elevated churn, rising support cost per account and a product roadmap being pulled in incoherent directions by customers who should never have bought. Product teams respond by improving retention, which is rational and ineffective, because the customers are not leaving due to a product deficiency; they are leaving because they were the wrong customers and the price told them they were the right ones. The tell that distinguishes this from ordinary churn is segmental: the churn is concentrated in cohorts acquired in the two quarters after a price or packaging change, and the exit interviews say some version of "we thought this was for companies like us."

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements are live among people who have done this work at scale, and none of them has been settled by evidence. Each is stated here in the form its strongest advocate would recognise.

Is the price the signal, or merely the headline on one?

The position argued through this page — that the price carries information only to the extent it is expensive to fake, and that the real signalling instruments are the commitments around it — has a serious opponent. The opposing view holds that in practice buyers almost never inspect the commitment structure; they see a number, form an impression in seconds, and rationalise afterwards. On this view the elaborate deterrence arithmetic of section 3 describes an equilibrium that theory requires and markets do not reach, and the practical lesson is simply that the number itself does the work. The evidence for it is real: the price–quality inference literature finds effects on perception from price alone, in controlled settings with no commitment structure present at all, and every practitioner has seen a price rise improve win rates in the same quarter it was implemented. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that those perception effects decay when the buyer has time, a committee and a procurement function — which is exactly the enterprise condition, and exactly where the evidence is thinnest.

Should prices be published?

The transparency camp holds that publishing the full price and discount schedule is dominant: it collapses dispersion, shortens cycles, removes the buyer's suspicion that someone else got a better deal, and converts every concession into a rule. Its evidence is the observed sales-cycle compression at companies that have done it and the well-documented corrosive effect of price opacity on trust. The opposing camp holds that heterogeneous buyers have genuinely different value realisation — a ₹1,500 crore conglomerate and a ₹200 crore manufacturer do not extract the same value from the same inspection system — and that published uniform pricing forfeits the surplus that funds the company's investment. Its evidence is the straightforward observation that almost no large enterprise software business publishes real enterprise prices, which is either a market failure or a revealed truth. What would have to be true for the transparency camp to be wrong: that the surplus forfeited exceeds the cycle-time and trust gains, which is measurable in principle and almost never measured in practice because running the counterfactual requires deliberately pricing two matched segments differently for several quarters.

Is usage-based pricing an honest signal or an admission?

One camp, now dominant in AI-native companies, holds that a usage or outcome metric is the only honest price because it aligns what the customer pays with what they receive and with what the seller spends. The other holds that usage pricing signals that the seller does not know what their product is worth and is transferring cost risk to a buyer who did not ask for it; that budget-holders hate unpredictable bills and will pay a premium for a cap; and that the most confident companies in any category charge a flat, legible price. Both positions are held by people with strong track records. What would have to be true for the usage camp to be wrong: that the predictability premium buyers pay for flat pricing exceeds the margin leakage from mismatched consumption — which is a measurable quantity that a company with both plans in market can estimate, and which very few have bothered to estimate.

Does signalling logic survive when buyers have good third-party information?

A sceptical position, increasingly well supported, is that price signalling is a theory of a world with poor information, and that review platforms, peer communities, public procurement data, analyst coverage and — more recently — buyers running their own evaluations of AI products with assistance from AI have eroded the asymmetry the theory depends on. On this view the correct forecast is that price inference weakens steadily and that companies investing in signalling are fighting the last war. The counter-position is that verification has improved for attributes and not for outcomes: a buyer can now verify a feature list in minutes and still cannot verify whether a system will work on their data in their plant with their people, which is the only thing that matters, and which remains as opaque as it was in 1973. This disagreement is the most consequential of the four, because the two views imply opposite investments — one in proof and evaluation infrastructure, the other in price and positioning — and it is genuinely unresolved.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can explain reference prices, congruence and the danger of discounting. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways, and the differences are behavioural rather than analytical.

They instrument the reference class. They do not guess what buyers compare them against; they have a field in the CRM for it, populated from discovery calls, and they review the distribution quarterly. When it shifts, they treat it as a market event on par with a competitor launch.

They read the realised distribution before the list price. Asked "what do you charge?", they answer with a mean and a spread, and they can decompose the spread by segment and channel. They regard a rising coefficient of variation as a defect with an owner, not as market softness.

They ship price changes and evidence in the same release. A price rise is never announced alone; it arrives with a commitment — a service level with a rupee penalty, a published uptime record, a named reference customer, an accuracy guarantee — so that the new number lands already underwritten. They know the deterrence arithmetic well enough to size the commitment, and they know to overshoot for enforceability.

They can name the last three deals they walked away from and the floor that they were protecting. They treat this as part of the pricing system rather than as sales discipline, and they make sure the walk-aways are visible internally, because a floor that the sales team does not believe in is not a floor.

They separate the authority question from the value question early. Before a long debate about what a buyer will pay, they establish who signs, at what threshold, and on which budget line — and they are willing to reshape a price to land on the right side of a threshold, while remaining honest with themselves that this is governance arbitrage and not value creation.

Finally, they hold the schools of section 2 simultaneously without pretending they agree. Asked why a particular number was chosen, an expert will say something like: "the level came from the value analysis, the shape came from the approval threshold, the guarantee came from the deterrence condition, and the framing came from the reference class — and where they conflicted, we chose the value analysis and accepted a longer cycle." That sentence, with its explicit acknowledgement of a trade-off actually made, is the clearest marker of command there is.

12. What they decided

Devika Nambiar took configuration D to Amritvela's board on 12 December 2026: hardware at ₹3.95 lakh per line, software at ₹3.20 lakh per line per year, a self-executing recall credit of ₹90,000 per quarter per line, and a two-axis discount table — term and line count, nothing else — published to channel partners with no field discretion below the floor. Her argument was not that ₹3.95 lakh was the right price. It was that the previous price had been making a claim Amritvela could not afford: that it was a capital-equipment vendor competing on instrument specification with importers who had forty years of balance sheet behind them. The new shape made a narrower and truer claim — a serious instrument with a service relationship — and the guarantee was what made the claim cost something to imitate. Arun Pillai's condition, which the board accepted, was that realised-price dispersion be reported to the board every quarter alongside bookings, on the grounds that the number the company defends in public is worth nothing if the number it accepts in private is drifting.

Zoya Kher launched the placement product at ₹2,400 on 1 February 2027 as a separately-named offering sold against coaching institutes rather than against apps, held ₹499 unchanged, and re-cut the free tier from ten conversations to twenty-five minutes of speech. Her reasoning was that Amiya had two products with two reference classes and had been trying to express both in one price ladder, which guaranteed that at least one of them would be misread. She declined, over her growth team's objection, to introduce an intermediate tier at ₹999, on the argument that a ladder of 0 / 499 / 999 / 2,400 would restore exactly the single-shelf reading she was trying to break. Nikhil Bose's condition was that the free tier's cost per user be reported weekly, and that any future free-tier limit be expressed in the unit that drives cost — a rule the company wrote down.

A price is a claim about identity, and a claim is worth only what it would cost to make falsely. The work of pricing is not choosing a number that sounds like who you are. It is building the commitments, the dispersion discipline and the cost structure that make the number expensive for anyone else to say.

Questions for discussion

  1. Amritvela set its hardware price at ₹3.95 lakh specifically to sit below a ₹4 lakh capital-approval threshold at a majority of its target accounts. Is this a legitimate act of product design, or is it arbitrage on a customer's internal governance that will be punished when the buyer notices? What would have to be true about Amritvela's economics for the answer to change?
  2. Amiya's free tier loses ₹126 lakh a month — nine times the combined contribution of both paid products — and is the reason the company has 1.9 lakh monthly users. At what point does a free tier stop being a growth investment and start being a price signal the company cannot afford to keep sending? What evidence would tell Kher she had passed that point, and would she be able to see it before her investors did?
  3. Amrai Naturals recovered its contribution in eighteen months but never recovered its realised price. If you accept Bhandari's framing — that the brand lost a sentence rather than a price — what is the general rule for when a promotional price is recoverable and when it is not? Test your rule against Amritvela and Amiya: could either of them run a five-week 40 percent promotion and recover?

13. Going deeper

  1. Packaging: good / better / best. The tier structure is the instrument through which a price signal is actually delivered in most software businesses; the ladder determines which number a buyer treats as the reference. Study it next because Kher's decision not to add a ₹999 tier only makes sense once you can reason about compromise and decoy effects in a ladder.
  2. Positioning. The reference class problem of section 6 is a positioning problem wearing a pricing costume. Positioning gives you the vocabulary and the method for choosing a comparison set deliberately rather than inheriting one.
  3. When to charge. The timing of the first payment is itself a signal — a card required at signup makes a very different claim from a fourteen-day trial or a paid pilot — and it interacts directly with the verification-cost condition C1 in Table 1.
  4. Willingness-to-pay research. Signalling tells you what a number implies; it cannot tell you what a segment can afford. Conjoint designs and Van Westendorp instruments are the standard tools, and knowing their contamination by anchoring effects is itself a mark of expertise.
  5. The value metric. The most consequential decision in the whole of pricing, and the one that determines whether your price scales with the customer's value or with your own cost. Amitava's shift from per-document to per-contract-value is a value-metric change, and everything else followed from it.
  6. Freemium vs free trial. Amiya's ₹126 lakh monthly free-tier bill is the general case of this question in an AI cost structure. The trade-off between a permanent free tier and a bounded trial is now an economic question as much as a growth one.
  7. AI cost-to-serve and pricing. Falling and volatile inference cost attacks price signals from underneath, and no stable practice has emerged. This is the topic where the field's open questions are most live and where the next five years of practice will be written.
  8. Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing. The three classical methods, and the discipline of knowing which one you are actually using. Most companies believe they price on value and in fact price on a competitor's number adjusted by a factor nobody can defend.

Uttung Hearing Care: Five Prices for One Device

Nashik, October 2026. A hearing-care chain must decide what to print on a price card — for a device four readers already price differently, and correctly.

1. Sunday night, Gangapur Road

At a quarter past nine on Sunday, 11 October 2026, the Uttung Hearing Care flagship on Gangapur Road in Nashik was empty but for its managing director. Manjiri Deore had spread five price cards on the fitting-room table, all printed by her own company within eleven months, each with a different number against one line: a mid-range receiver-in-canal hearing aid her stock system called the U7.

₹74,500 an ear was the all-in Dhaancha Complete price — trial, real-ear verification, eight tuning visits over two years, remote fine-tuning, loss cover. ₹62,000 was the unbundled clinic price: device plus one fitting. ₹41,000 was a private health insurer's approved rate, offered to Uttung as a network provider from 1 December. ₹38,900 was where an online seller authorised by the manufacturer's Indian arm had listed the identical model since March. ₹24,000 was Uttung's rate under a Nashik industrial trust's corporate-social-responsibility programme.

The spread was 3.1 times, and none of the five was a discount or a mistake; each had been negotiated, costed and signed by somebody who could defend it. On Tuesday, 20 October the cards went to the printer for all thirty-four clinics; before that, on Friday the 16th, she had to answer the insurer. She no longer knew which of the five numbers her company was asking the market to believe.

2. How Uttung came to have five prices

Manjiri Deore and Dhananjay Baviskar opened the first clinic in Nashik in 2009. Six clinics and the free camps followed by 2014; franchising began in Malegaon in 2017. By March 2026 there were thirty-four clinics — eleven in Nashik, five in Ahmednagar, three in Sangamner, four in Malegaon, five in Dhule, six in Jalgaon — twenty-one owned, thirteen franchised, fifty-eight audiologists, turnover just under ₹50 crore (Exhibit 1).

Two earlier decisions shaped what was possible. The first, in 2019, was the Dhaancha protocol: a fourteen-step fitting and verification discipline Dhananjay wrote and Manjiri decided to price rather than advertise. Uttung began selling fittings rather than devices at one all-in price, believing that would end comparison. Instead it created a second, lower price for patients who refused the bundle, and handed their adult children a subtraction to perform.

The second was the April 2021 distribution agreement with a global manufacturer's Indian subsidiary, which gave Uttung a landed cost of ₹18,400 on the U7 class against a list cost of ₹24,900. In exchange, clause 4.2 set a minimum annual offtake of 5,200 units, clause 6.5 forbade publishing below ₹41,000, and clause 7.1 let the manufacturer appoint authorised online sellers. In 2021 that last clause looked theoretical. In March 2026 it stopped being theoretical.

3. The industry a price has to speak to

India fits a small fraction of the hearing aids it needs, almost all of them out of pocket. Hearing aids attract nil GST, so Uttung has never explained tax on a device — but service sold separately would be taxable at 18 per cent, a point its Nashik auditor had begun to raise about the Dhaancha bundle. Devices are notified under the Medical Devices Rules and imported against CDSCO licences. At the bottom of the market ADIP and ALIMCO supply basic behind-the-ear aids for a few thousand rupees, indicatively around ₹3,700 — the anchor many patients carry into a private clinic.

Above that sit the private chains: hospital departments at Apollo and Fortis, a long tail of single-clinic audiologists, and a growing shadow of e-commerce. Lenskart's move into hearing has made investors ask the same question about scale. Amazon and Flipkart carry hundreds of amplification devices, most not hearing aids in any clinical sense — and, since March, the model Uttung fits.

Uttung's exposure abroad is small but load-bearing. Its outcome analytics ride on a fitting-software platform whose clinical lead, Nuria Ferrer, works from Valencia. Its proposed own-brand entry line would be built in Kuala Lumpur, where Farid Azman had quoted ₹6,300 an aid for eighteen months. Its data lead, Utkarsha Bhamare, is in Pune.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In January 2024 a Nashik industrial trust agreed to fund U7 fittings for low-income patients referred by hospital ENTs, at ₹24,000 an aid plus a programme fee; everyone believed the rate was contribution-positive. In July 2026 a costing review by Digambar Nikam put the variable cost of a U7 fitting outside the bundle at ₹24,200 — device ₹18,400, fitting and verification ₹4,500, warranty support ₹1,300 — so each scheme fitting lost ₹200 before overhead. Six hundred and ninety were done that year.

In March 2026 an authorised online seller listed the U7 at ₹38,900, device only, against Uttung's contractual floor of ₹41,000. The manufacturer's position, put politely and repeatedly, was that marketplace festival funding explained the gap and nothing it or its distributors published had breached anything. Uttung's clinics began quietly matching: 620 ears in the year.

In August the insurer's invitation arrived. Its approved rate of ₹41,000 sat exactly on the contractual floor, and the condition was rate parity: the network rate had to be Uttung's published rate in every channel. There was no room to go lower, and none to keep ₹62,000.

Then two things arrived in one September week. Nuria Ferrer's outcome pack (Exhibit 5) showed the cheapest cohort wearing their aids longest and returning them least. And Digambar's team, asked the price of a U7, produced three defensible answers (Exhibit 3). On 25 September Dr Madhuri Ahirrao, an ENT surgeon in Jalgaon who had referred patients for eleven years, telephoned to ask whether Uttung had become a discount shop: a Malegaon franchise had run a Navratri offer at ₹39,900 on its own signage, and a competitor had photographed it.

8. The options as Manjiri sees them

Option 1: hold. Keep ₹74,500 and ₹62,000, decline the insurer, let clinics match online where they must. Contribution ₹1,821.12 lakh, nothing to explain to Dr Ahirrao, and a slow leak: 900 ears matched to ₹38,900 next year against 620 this, and no rule on who may match.

Option 2: parity. Sign at ₹41,000, publish it everywhere, sell the Dhaancha service separately at ₹19,500 including tax. The best contribution in the exhibit, ₹1,890.32 lakh, and the only option with no contingent GST or offtake exposure. It needs eleven audiologists Uttung does not have in districts that produced nine graduates last year, and prints the number that makes 47 per cent of ENTs suspicious.

Option 3: one price only. Abolish the unbundled price, publish ₹74,500 and nothing else, refuse to match, decline the insurer. The cleanest signal and the smallest business: 3,900 ears, a breach of clause 4.2, a contingent ₹253.50 lakh.

Option 4: segment. Keep the U7 clinic-only, withdraw it wherever Uttung can, and launch Farid Azman's entry line at ₹19,900 for camps, the CSR programme and marketplaces. Best contribution before contingencies, ₹1,951.10 lakh, at 95.7 per cent chair-hour use with two Malegaon clinics already short of an audiologist. Also a ₹19,900 device with Uttung's name on it, which is a signal too.

All four share an assumption Manjiri had written on a card and turned face down: that Uttung sets the price a patient sees. It does not. The marketplace listing is the manufacturer's to appoint, the ₹41,000 the insurer's and the contract's, the ₹24,000 the trust's, the ₹39,900 Zeba Momin's. All four are also about the price of a device, while what a patient consumes over two years is mostly service — and Exhibit 3 shows Uttung cannot say what it charges for either.

Friday, 16 October: the network agreement, or no December listing. Tuesday, 20 October: cards to the printer.
